reason: The text consistently portrays the Hebrews as a collective nation rather than merely a family or individual followers. Key evidence includes: (1) repeated use of 'בְּנֵי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל' (benei Yisrael - 'children of Israel/Israelites'), a national collective designation; (2) God explicitly refers to them as 'עַמִּי' (ammi - 'my people'), establishing them as a nation; (3) their shared national experience is emphasized—'צַעֲקַת בְּנֵי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל' (the cry of the children of Israel) and their collective affliction by Egypt (הַלַּחַץ אֲשֶׁר מִצְרַיִם לֹחֲצִים אֹתָם); (4) the narrative describes national liberation ('הוֹצֵא אֶת־ עַמִּי בְנֵי־ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרָיִם' - 'bring out my people, the children of Israel, from Egypt'); and (5) they are called to a collective national purpose ('תַּעַבְדוּן אֶת־ הָאֱלֹהִים עַל הָהָר הַזֶּה' - serve God on the mountain). While patriarchal lineage is also mentioned, the text emphasizes the Israelites as an organized people and nation beyond familial bonds.
